::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
This is an agenda item and not a proposal. It states a gap that is measured and real, and then
says why the study it implies cannot be run from public data. It is published so that the gap
is on the record rather than quietly skipped because it is inconvenient.
:::

## The measurement

Of the 1830 articles in the corpus, four carry a publication type of randomized controlled
trial, controlled clinical trial or clinical trial:

| PMID | year | article |
|---|---|---|
| 36995753 | 2023 | Using normative language when describing scientific findings: randomized controlled trial |
| 35838202 | 2022 | Selective outcome reporting in paediatric dentistry restorative treatment randomized clinical trials |
| 34118367 | 2021 | The impact of gender on researchers' assessment: a randomized controlled trial |
| 29886846 | 2018 | Avoidable waste of research related to outcome planning and reporting in clinical trials |

Of those four, two are experiments on the research process itself: the normative language trial
and the gender assessment trial. The other two carry the type because the object they studied
was a trial, not because they ran one.

Two experiments in 1830 articles. The corpus is 549 meta-epidemiological studies, 680 that
examine systematic reviews, and almost no manipulation of anything.

## Why this matters rather than merely being true

Meta-research grades other fields on their evidence hierarchy. It tells clinical researchers
that an observational association is weaker than a randomized comparison, and it is right. Its
own output is almost entirely observational association.

Some of that is unavoidable. You cannot randomize whether a paper was preregistered. But the
questions the field most wants answered are causal and several of them are randomizable: whether
a reporting checklist at submission improves reporting, whether blinding reviewers changes what
gets accepted, whether a data availability mandate produces available data or only statements.
Each of those is an intervention on a process someone controls.

## Why it cannot be run here

Every such experiment requires randomizing something inside a journal, a funder or an ethics
committee: which manuscripts get an intervention, which reviewers see what, which applicants
receive which instruction. None of that is reachable from public data, and no amount of
harvesting substitutes for the permission.

The honest statement is that this project can measure the gap and cannot fill it. Recording
that is more useful than inventing an observational proxy and calling it an answer, which is
precisely the substitution the field is criticized for elsewhere.

## What would make it runnable

A partner willing to randomize one thing: a journal, a preprint server, a funder, or a
conference with a submission process. The design is not the obstacle and would be short. The
access is the obstacle.

## The one caveat on the measurement

Publication type is assigned by NLM indexing and an experiment can be missed. 515 of the corpus
records carry no MeSH indexing at all, mostly the most recent, and an unindexed experiment would
not appear in the count above. The number is a floor, not a point estimate, and the floor is
four.
